studies.Population: AGES-Reykjavik cohort of older Icelandic men
studies.Reference: Rye bread consumption in early life and reduced risk of advanced prostate cancer.
studies.Authors: Torfadottir JE, Valdimarsdottir UA, Mucci L, Stampfer M, Kasperzyk JL, Fall K, Tryggvadottir L, Aspelund T, Olafsson O, Harris TB, Jonsson E, Tulinius H, Adami HO, Gudnason V, Steingrimsdottir L
studies.direction_imputation_reason: Comparison direction was not explicit; the protocol assumes high versus low exposure.
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Dietary habits were assessed for early-, mid- , and current life using a validated food frequency questionnaire (FFQ).

sample_size.excerpt: The current analysis is based on those men responding to questions on early life rye bread consumption (n = 2,258), midlife rye bread consumption (n = 2,260), early life oatmeal consumption (n = 2,255), midlife oatmeal consumption (n = 2,259) and midlife whole wheat bread consumption (n =2,255).

effect_size.excerpt: ≤4 times/ week) was not associated with risk of prostate cancer diagnosis (OR = 0.99, 95% CI: 0.77-1.27), nor statistically significant with advanced prostate cancer (OR = 0.67, 95% CI: 0.37-1.20). High intake of oatmeal in midlife was not associated with prostate cancer risk and neither was current intake for either total prostate cancer (HR = 1.06, 95% CI: 0.74-1.52) nor advanced disease (HR = 0.99, 95% CI: 0.44-2.23).

confidence_interval.excerpt: ≤4 times/ week) was not significantly associated with risk of PCa diagnosis (OR = 0.99, 95% CI: 0.77-1.27) nor advanced PCa (OR = 0.67, 95% CI: 0.37-1.20).

comparison.excerpt: High intake of oatmeal in adolescence (≥5 vs. ≤4 times/ week)

design.excerpt: In 2002 to 2006, 2,268 men, aged 67-96 years, reported their dietary habits in the AGES-Reykjavik cohort study.

timing.excerpt: In this study we investigated whether whole-grain consumption in different periods of life is associated with risk of prostate cancer in adult life in a prospective cohort study.

continent.excerpt: In Iceland, rye and oatmeal were the main types of whole-grain in the diet during the first half of the 20 th century.
